“Perhaps we can trace it back to the level of technology through which Nyaya thinkers tried to understand the problem of creation.

“As we noted earlier, they understood the creation of a thing as the result of bringing together the parts from which it is made. Their standard example was the production of a pot by joining its parts together. This method of production is called kabala and is still used in our country in pottery.

“Because the followers of Nyaya tried to understand the production of everything through this same model, they also explained the creation of things made from atoms as basically a process of combining atoms.
“But if this is a process of bringing things together, then there must be someone who brings them together.
“In this way, a place was opened within the Nyaya system for ‘God,’ who was called upon to fill this gap in the atomic hypothesis.”
10 — The Relationship Between Material and Intellectual Production

There is no doubt that Chattopadhyaya’s way of framing the question deserves attention. But if we look at the issue more broadly, on the level of society as a whole, it is useful to remember what Marx said on this subject:

“Historical periods differ from one another not in what they produce, but in how they produce it. So there is nothing unreasonable about connecting the way ideas are produced with the way material goods are produced.”

Of course, it would be wrong to derive the way ideas are produced—and especially their content—mechanically from the way material goods are produced. This does not mean rejecting Chattopadhyaya’s conclusion. But we do need to add the influence of earlier ideas and intellectual traditions, above all religious traditions, which have always had, and still have, an especially powerful influence on Indian culture.

We should also remember that mystical theories did not develop in a vacuum. They too were shaped by a whole range of political and intellectual traditions. Even Epicurus, despite his reputation for atheism, still spoke about the gods. In Indian philosophy, religious traditions were much stronger. Alongside changes in technology, these traditions were among the factors that helped change the form taken by atomism in the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika school.
In explaining how the followers of this school understood divine intervention in the movement of atoms, the Indian philosopher Shastri writes:

“The atomic theory of the Nyāya system included the assumption that the will of almighty God awakens in the atoms the necessary effects of the actions and conduct of the souls, or jīvas, that reside in bodies. It also awakens in them different kinds of activity connected with the qualities inherent in the atoms. Under the influence of this activity, atoms join together in pairs, groups of three, groups of four, and so on. Creation (sṛṣṭi) takes place in this way. If the jīvas no longer require creation in this form, the almighty will of God produces other kinds of activity in the atoms. These cause them to split apart, destroying the forces that hold two atoms together in a pair, and the atomic combinations then dissolve, beginning with the pair.”

We have gone into this much detail about Greek and Indian atomic theories for a deliberate reason. These are the two main ancient sources of atomism, and we wanted to present them clearly enough, both historically and scientifically, to make a serious comparison possible between them and the atomic theories found in the Arab-Islamic intellectual tradition.
Only then can we make a sound judgment about the older sources from which Arab atomists may have borrowed, or drawn inspiration, when developing theories of their own.
We might even say that this detailed account of Greek and Indian atomism helps fill a gap in modern Arab knowledge of the subject.
After this extended overview of atomic theories in ancient philosophy, one further comparison may help complete the picture: the difference between ancient and modern ideas about the atom.
The first thing that stands out is one basic difference between the ancient view and the modern one. It may even be the decisive difference.

Ancient thinkers—Democritus above all—believed that division must eventually reach a final point, beyond which the atom could no longer be divided. Modern science, by contrast, has shown through experiment that the atom can continue to be divided without such a final limit.

There is another difference as well. Ancient theories did not solve the problem of what holds the parts of an atom together, or what holds atoms together when they form different combinations. Different answers were proposed, but none reached the heart of the problem. On this point, they all remained trapped within a rather simple way of thinking.

Modern science, by contrast, was able to solve the problem through the development of experimental methods and technology. It showed that when atoms meet, they bind together through chemical affinities that arise between them.

Yet despite the many deep differences between ancient and modern thought in this field, we still have to recognize that modern chemistry and physics rest, at a fundamental level, on Democritus’s theory and developed from the assumptions with which he began.

In the nineteenth century, Cournot wrote in his Study of the Sequence of Fundamental Ideas in the Sciences and in History (p. 245) that no idea inherited from antiquity had reached anything like the importance of Democritus’s idea of the atom.

Galileo almost certainly knew the teachings of Democritus. Pierre Gassendi, who helped bring atomic theory into modern science, began from his study of Epicurus, the great continuator of Democritus. Even Descartes, who rejected atomic theory, was so deeply influenced by Democritus in his mechanical explanation of nature that, in a letter to Mersenne dated 30 August 1640, he had to answer the accusation that he had done little more than patch up the worn-out clothes of Democritus.
We should also mention what Kedrov wrote about atomism in the Great Soviet Encyclopedia:

“The view that atoms never change, that they are incapable of development or qualitative transformation, that the relations between them are purely external and mechanical, and that they possess no motion except mechanical motion—this is the view characteristic of the metaphysical and mechanical conception of atoms, that is, of old atomism.

“The dialectical conception of atoms, confirmed by modern science, is characterized instead by the view that atoms are capable of change, that they form a successive series of stages of development that grow qualitatively more complex, that they continually enter into both organic and inorganic combinations governed by definite patterns, and that they are in permanent and uninterrupted motion.”
E — The Atomic Question in Arab-Islamic Thought
We have now reached the point toward which this long discussion of the different ancient forms of atomism has been leading.

Our aim is to identify the source from which Arab-Islamic thought took the basic elements of atomism and then brought them into Islamic theological debate, reshaping them according to its own outlook and giving them a largely independent character.
There are two questions we need to examine.

The first is the source used by the earliest Arab-Islamic thinker to introduce the idea of the “indivisible part” into Islamic thought. As we have already seen, that thinker was Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf.

We put the question this way because scientific research cannot reasonably assume that al-ʿAllāf began thinking about the “indivisible part,” or the “indivisible substance,” in complete isolation from the theories that had existed for more than a thousand years before him.

Those theories had developed among peoples whose cultures, especially their philosophical traditions, had by al-ʿAllāf’s time come into extensive contact with Arab-Islamic thought, though the depth of that contact differed from one culture to another.

We also know from al-ʿAllāf’s own life that he had encountered forms of foreign philosophical knowledge that had become available to Arab thinkers in his time. These ideas had entered the wider Arab intellectual movement and were already having a visible effect on its rapid development.
In short, no researcher taking a scientific approach can easily believe that al-ʿAllāf discovered atomic theory entirely on his own, independently of everything known by the ancient philosophers.
There must therefore have been some earlier model of the theory—drawn from one or another of the ancient traditions we have already discussed—on which he built his own thinking.

The second question is how the theory of the “indivisible part” entered Muʿtazilite thought, how the Muʿtazilites used it in arguing for the central principles of their school, and what kind of character the theory acquired in their hands.
As for the source from which al-ʿAllāf and the other Muʿtazilites—and later the Ashʿarites—took the basic theory, we cannot reach a final and certain conclusion.
But we can weigh the different possibilities in the light of the clear evidence provided by historical reality.
On this basis, the Greek source seems to us the most likely direct model from which these thinkers first began, especially the pioneer in this field, al-ʿAllāf.
We base this judgment on two considerations.

The first is that Indian philosophy in general—let alone the detailed teachings and theories of its different schools—was still only poorly known to Arabs in al-ʿAllāf’s lifetime, between the eighth and ninth centuries CE.
Fragments of Indian culture had reached them, usually through Persian intermediaries, but they had arrived in a scattered and unsystematic form.

Even the Muslim historian al-Qifṭī, who wrote well after the ninth century and whose historical works include The History of the Wise—a work closer to a history of philosophy than to general history—could still say:
“Because India is so far from our lands, few of their writings have reached us. Only fragments of their sciences have come to us, and we have heard of only a small number of their scholars.”

Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī did present examples of Indian religious philosophy in his famous book Verification of What India Says. But that book appeared much later than the time of al-ʿAllāf, in the eleventh century.
It is therefore difficult for a researcher to suppose that al-ʿAllāf knew the atomic theory of Indian philosophy, or at least that he knew it as clearly as he knew Greek atomic theory.

We have little doubt that he had access to enough material to gain a reasonably coherent understanding of Democritus’s theory, even if this came not through direct sources—which seems unlikely—but indirectly.

Al-ʿAllāf lived for about a hundred years, from 135 to 235 AH. Those hundred years covered both the first and second major periods in which Greek science and philosophy were translated into Arabic, or transmitted through summaries, explanations, and commentaries.
During this period, thinkers in Abbasid Arab society became familiar with the theories of many ancient Greek philosophers.
We know for certain that they knew Aristotle, at the very least.
As we saw earlier, Aristotle wrote about the views of Leucippus and Democritus on the full and the void, one of the most important foundations of their atomic theory.
We also know that Arabs of the period had access to an Arabic translation of Aristotle’s Metaphysics, which contains substantial discussion of Democritus’s atomism.
There is another point as well. Most historians of the Islamic schools, including al-Shahrastānī, report that al-ʿAllāf took his ideas about the divine attributes from Greek philosophers.
This means that his familiarity with Greek philosophy was taken for granted by these historians. They had no serious doubt about it.
His familiarity with Indian philosophy, by contrast, is much less certain.

None of the early historians of Arab philosophy said anything about a connection between the atomism of al-ʿAllāf and other Arab-Islamic thinkers and Indian atomism. Some Orientalist scholars later suggested such a connection, but without providing convincing historical or scientific evidence for it.

The French Orientalist Henry Corbin, for example, discussed the Ashʿarite idea of the creation of the world and the relationship it implies between the Creator and the universe. He wrote that the Ashʿarites found a “foundation and justification” for their view:

“in their theory of the indivisible substance, or the indivisible part, which is what is known as atomism. This theory was known in ancient times among Greek and Indian thinkers, but the Ashʿarites developed and explained it according to their own philosophical tendencies, so that the consequences of the theory would support their views about infinite divine power and creation.”
But this is only a passing reference to the Greek and Indian sources together. Corbin makes no attempt to define the exact relationship between either source and Ashʿarite theory.

The Orientalist S. Pines did try to make that connection more precise. He argued that Indian atomism was the source used by al-ʿAllāf and the other Muslim thinkers who accepted the theory of the indivisible part.
But his argument did not produce convincing proof. It rested largely on interpretation and personal inference rather than on historical analysis.
There is also a useful observation in Goldziher’s discussion of Indian influences on Muslims. He says that the influence of Indian Buddhism on them was only secondary.

By Buddhism here, he cannot simply mean Buddhism as a religion in itself, nor only its purely theological side stripped of its philosophical ideas. As we saw earlier in our discussion of Indian atomism, the theory itself had roots in early Buddhist belief.
The second consideration is the character of Greek philosophical thought itself.

Its strongly rational and logical character was the dominant model among Arab theoretical thinkers, and among Muslim thinkers more generally, in al-ʿAllāf’s time. This same character is clearly visible in al-ʿAllāf’s own thought.
It also seems that these thinkers regarded Indian philosophy as lacking the kind of rational and logical character that fascinated them and gave their own theoretical work its distinctive shape.
In our view, this impression among Arab and other Muslim thinkers of the period had two main causes.

First, as we have already said, logical and rational thought had become dominant in their own intellectual work during the flourishing of the Abbasid scientific revival in the third and fourth Islamic centuries.

Second, while they were themselves working in this rational style, it seems that the part of Indian thought familiar to them came mainly through Persian Gnostics and consisted largely of its spiritual and contemplative side.
If our estimate is correct, this gives further support to the view that they did not yet know the atomic theory of Indian philosophy.
Strangely enough, Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī came along in the fifth Islamic century—the eleventh century CE—and confirmed this impression of Indian thought in very broad terms.

He wrote his famous book on India after spending forty years there in scholarly study. Yet even he criticized the method of Indian scholars and philosophers as unscientific. He argued that their knowledge had not freed itself from superstition, and that what was found in their books was like:
“shells mixed with pottery, pearls mixed with dung, or fine steeds mixed with pebbles. To them the two things are alike, because they have no path by which to rise to the level of demonstration.”
It is also striking that the same impression of ancient Indian thought passed from early Arab thinkers to modern Arab researchers.
We can see it clearly even in a scholar known for his care and precision, Aḥmad Amīn.
When discussing Indian culture, its influence on Arab culture, and the relationship between Greek and Indian metaphysical philosophy, he writes:

“Indian philosophy became completely mixed with religion and took on a poetic rather than a scientific character. It did not move step by step from what can be sensed to what can be understood by reason. In many cases it was content with poetic expression full of metaphors, images, and imaginative language, instead of following the scientific method, which requires explanation through facts rather than metaphors.”
He then identifies another difference between the two traditions. Indian philosophy, he says:

“defined the purpose of philosophy as serving the human being, whereas Greek philosophy sought knowledge for its own sake. The main motive of Indian philosophy was the human longing for release from the pains and hardships of this world. Among the Greeks, the first motive of philosophy was wonder: wonder at the appearances of the world, which led people to seek to understand them and thus to philosophize.”
Our purpose here is not to debate Aḥmad Amīn’s judgment.
What matters to us is the persistence of this view among Arab researchers, both ancient and modern, and what we can draw from it for the question before us.

The persistence of this view is itself one useful sign supporting our conclusion that the Greek source, rather than the Indian one, was the direct model from which atomism first entered Arab-Islamic thought.
The situation is different when we turn to Persian Gnostic and Manichaean sources.

Here we cannot claim that Arab thinkers in the age of Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf knew little about them. Intellectual and historical evidence strongly suggests the opposite: that these thinkers knew a great deal about such movements, and that some of them were even influenced by certain parts of their beliefs and ideas.
But the issue before us concerns Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite thinkers.
Despite the major differences between these two schools, both stood very far from the basic ideas and assumptions of Gnosticism and Manichaeism.
The Gnostic and Manichaean theories of the basic elements of the universe rested on a dualistic view of its origin.

This was fundamentally incompatible with the Muʿtazilites in particular, because they insisted so strongly on divine transcendence: God had to be kept completely free of anything that might cast even the slightest shadow over the principle of divine unity as they understood it.
Since we consider Greek atomic theory the most likely source used by the Muʿtazilites, we can now move to our second task: comparing Greek atomism with the atomic theory of the Muʿtazilites.

This will help us see how they used the theory of Democritus in their own system, and how they made its early materialist and dialectical tendencies fit with their own idealist and metaphysical starting points.
We will naturally begin with al-ʿAllāf, since he was the first Muʿtazilite to adopt the theory of the indivisible part.

After that we will turn to the Ashʿarites, who made the theory one of the basic foundations of their argument for the existence and eternity of God the Creator, and for the claim that the world itself came into existence later.
Before beginning the comparison, however, we should stress a point already mentioned at the start of our discussion of atomism.

When Muʿtazilite thinkers, beginning with al-ʿAllāf, and later the Ashʿarites took up this question, their aim was not to study the natural world for its own sake, as the Greek philosophers had done in their philosophy of nature.
Al-ʿAllāf, the first Arab-Islamic thinker to take up the question, was not trying to build a theory of nature or of the material world.

His aim and motive remained entirely within the same metaphysical world that formed the general framework of Muʿtazilite thought, just as it had formed the general framework of other Muslim thinkers before Arab philosophy emerged as an independent discipline.
